stories.title_en: Boatmen Abscond with a Servant and the Baggage

paragraphs.zh: 倪典史以吏员出身，家实巨富。初受官，将赴新任，在京置买器用什物、珍玩缎匹，色色美丽，装作行李六担。打点俱备，先遣三个家人押往江边搭船，以一家人在船中守护，其二人复归。次日，同倪典史大伙人俱到江边寻船，并不见前船；其守船家人不知载在何去，知被贼艄所拐矣。
paragraphs.en: Assistant Magistrate Ni had risen from the clerical ranks; the family was in fact hugely rich. On first receiving office, about to go to his new post, he bought in the capital utensils and household goods, curios, and bolts of silk, every kind fine and beautiful, packed as six loads of luggage. When everything was ready, he first sent three servants to the river to hire a boat; one servant stayed on the boat to watch, and the other two came back. The next day Assistant Magistrate Ni and the rest of the party all went to the river to look for the boat, and the earlier boat was nowhere to be seen. The servant who had been watching the boat had been carried off no one knew where; they knew a thief of a boatman had abducted them.

paragraphs.zh: 倪典史不得已，复入京城，向乡知借觅盘缠，欲往在京衙门告捕船贼。同选乡友阻之曰：“凡讨船须在捕头写定，其舵公有姓名可查，方保稳当。若自向江头讨船，彼此不相识，来历无可查，安得不致失误？且江边常有贼船，舵公伪装商贾，打听某船有好货，多致江中劫掠者，皆是在头查访去。若不识者，误上他船，虽主人亦同被害，何况载走一仆乎！今你赴任有限期，岂能在此久待？船贼又无名姓踪影，虽告何从追捕？不如罢休。”倪典史依劝，复在京中再置切要之物，急往赴任也。此不识写船而致误者，故述为舟行之戒。
paragraphs.en: Assistant Magistrate Ni had no choice but to go back into the capital and borrow travel money from fellow provincials, intending to file a charge at a capital yamen and have the boat thieves caught. Fellow new appointees stopped him, saying: “Whenever you hire a boat you should register it at the licensed wharf office, so the helmsman has a name that can be looked up; only then is it safe. If you hire a boat yourself at the river’s edge, neither side knows the other, and there is no origin to check—how can you not come to grief? Besides, there are often thief-boats along the river. Helmsmen disguise themselves as merchants, find out which boat has good cargo, and many then rob it mid-river—those are all cases of failing to check at the office first. If you do not know this and board their boat by mistake, even the master himself may be harmed with them—how much more when they carry off one servant! You have a deadline to take up your post; how can you wait here long? The boat thieves have no names or traces; even if you file a charge, from where would you hunt them? Better drop it.” Assistant Magistrate Ni followed the advice, bought the most needful things again in the capital, and hurried off to his post. This is a case of not knowing how to book a boat, and so coming to grief; I record it as a warning for those who travel by water.

stories.title_en: The Bride Escapes the Boat by Night

paragraphs.zh: 扬州有一危棍，以骗局为生。生一女危氏，美貌聪明，年方二八，尚未字人。同帮计棍，青年伶俐，家无父母，危棍因以女招赘为婿。夫妻欢爱，岳婿同心。
paragraphs.en: In Yangzhou there was a crook named Wei, who lived by swindles. He had a daughter, Miss Wei, pretty and clever, just sixteen, not yet betrothed. A partner in the same trade, Crook Ji, was a young man of ready wits, with no parents at home; Crook Wei therefore took him as a live-in son-in-law. Husband and wife loved each other, and father-in-law and son-in-law were of one mind.

paragraphs.zh: 后半年内，无甚生意。适有贾知县新受官赴任，经过扬州，欲娶一妾。危与计私议，欲以女脱嫁之。计许诺，自为媒，往与贾爷议。来看称意，即行聘礼，受银八十两，择日成婚。危与计同对女曰：“今半年无生意，家用穷迫，故以你假嫁与贾知县。其实你夫少年人，何忍舍你？我为父母，止生你一人，何忍舍你去？只不得已，把你为货也。况贾爷年老，他眼下未带长妻来，自然爱惜你。但恐到任后，接长妻到，必然酷虐你，骂詈鞭挞，自是不免。自古道：‘宁作贫人妻，莫作贵人妾’。今暂送你去，不日即登船矣。你夫暗以船随行，其船夜挂一白裤为号。你夜间若可逃，即逃过白裤船来，夫即在接你矣。切莫贪睡，误你夫终身；且你自受苦楚。”计故挽妻衣，涕泣面恳曰：“你肯许归，任你去；若不能逃，吾宁与你同死，决不忍相舍。”危氏亦泣曰：“父母有命，怎的不归？只你要随船候接，不可耽误。”三人商议已定。
paragraphs.en: For half a year after that there was little business. It happened that Magistrate Jia, newly appointed and on his way to his post, passed through Yangzhou and wanted to take a concubine. Wei and Ji talked it over in private, and wanted to fake-marry the daughter to him. Ji agreed, acted as matchmaker himself, and went to discuss it with His Honor Jia. Jia came to look, was pleased, sent betrothal gifts at once, paid eighty taels, and chose a day for the wedding. Wei and Ji together said to the daughter: “We have had no business for half a year; the household is hard pressed, so we are fake-marrying you to Magistrate Jia. In truth your husband is a young man—how could he bear to give you up? We are your parents, and we have only you—how could we bear to let you go? We simply have no choice; we are using you as goods. Besides, His Honor Jia is old; he has not brought his principal wife with him for now, so of course he will cherish you. But I fear that after he takes up his post and sends for the principal wife, she will surely treat you cruelly; cursing and whipping will be hard to avoid. The old saying goes: ‘Better a poor man’s wife than a rich man’s concubine.’ For now we will send you; in a few days he will board a boat. Your husband will secretly follow in a boat, with a white pair of trousers hung up as a signal. If you can flee at night, flee across to the white-trousers boat; your husband will be there to take you. Do not sleep greedily and ruin your husband’s whole life; you yourself would also suffer.” Ji deliberately clutched his wife’s clothes, weeping, and pleaded to her face: “If you will promise to come back, I will let you go; if you cannot flee, I would rather die with you—I cannot bear to part.” Miss Wei also wept and said: “When father and mother have given the order, how would I not come back? Only you must follow in a boat and wait to take me; do not miss the time.” The three of them had the plan set.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，贾知县遣人迎婚，计为媒送去，贾与危氏在店成亲。又次日，危亦备席待婿，兼为起程。第四日，贾同妻收拾上船，危、计二人送别殷勤。船行一日无恙，次日泊于洲渚。计暗以船随，挨附其旁，挂一白裤于上。危氏同贾夫出船头观玩，见白裤船在旁，知计夫在候矣。夜与贾宿，着意绸缪，尽云雨之欢。贾以暮年新娶，夜夜不虚；况此夜船中又尽兴一次，帖然鼾睡矣。危氏遂密起，爬过有白裤船。计夫早已在候，相见欢甚，正似花再重开月再圆也。夤夜撑船逃回。
paragraphs.en: The next day Magistrate Jia sent men to receive the bride. Ji as matchmaker saw her off; Jia and Miss Wei consummated the marriage at an inn. The day after that, Wei also laid a feast for his son-in-law, and for the start of the journey as well. On the fourth day Jia and his wife packed and boarded; Wei and Ji saw them off with great care. The boat went one day without incident. The next day it moored at a sandbar. Ji secretly followed in a boat, drew up alongside, and hung a white pair of trousers on it. Miss Wei went out to the bow with husband Jia to look about, saw the white-trousers boat beside them, and knew husband Ji was waiting. That night she slept with Jia, put her whole mind to tenderness, and they made love to the full. Jia was old and newly married, and had not missed a night; besides, this night on the boat he spent himself once more, and then slept snoring soundly. Miss Wei then rose in secret, crawled across to the boat with the white trousers. Husband Ji had long been waiting; they were overjoyed to see each other, just as if the flower had opened again and the moon were round once more. In the night they poled away and fled home.

paragraphs.zh: 次早，贾知县醒来，不见危氏，心甚疑怪。再差一家人，往危老家报。危家惊异，疑是船中乖争，致逼投水，即赴府具状，告苛逼溺命事。家人数日回报，贾知县欲赴任期，不能久待，亦不往诉辨，自径投任去。三年后，入京朝觐，差家人送些少仪物与危老，见其家有一少妇，抱一幼子，宛似危氏，驰归报主。及贾知县打轿往，并不见踪。问昨妇何人，危云：“妻姨之女。”其妻反出来涕泣诘骂，扭问取人，又被骗银十两，方得脱身。此误娶棍女而人财两空，又受尽多少闲气也。
paragraphs.en: The next morning Magistrate Jia woke and did not see Miss Wei; he was much puzzled and suspicious. He then sent a servant to report it at Old Wei’s house. The Wei family acted startled, and suspected a quarrel on the boat had driven her to throw herself in the water. They went at once to the prefecture and filed a charge of cruelty driving a person to drown. After several days the servant came back to report. Magistrate Jia had a deadline to take up his post and could not wait long; he did not go to plead his side, but went straight to his post. Three years later he went to the capital for the imperial audience, and sent a servant with a few ceremonial gifts to Old Wei. The servant saw that the house had a young woman holding a small child, the very image of Miss Wei, and galloped back to tell his master. When Magistrate Jia went in a sedan, there was no trace of her. He asked who yesterday’s woman was; Wei said: “My wife’s sister’s daughter.” Wei’s wife then came out weeping, questioning and cursing, twisting him to produce the person; he was cheated of another ten taels before he could get away. This is a case of wrongly taking a crook’s daughter: he lost both the person and the money, and swallowed no small amount of idle abuse besides.

paragraphs.zh: 按：娶妾于妻岳之家，既在店成亲，又送别登舟，可谓极稳矣。谁知在船后，夜复能逃？故在外娶妾，不唯审择外家，兼亦宜审媒人居止，及靠店家一同核实，方可无失。然大抵不及娶本地人女，为更稳也。
paragraphs.en: Note: He took a concubine from the girl’s father’s house; they consummated the marriage at an inn, and were even seen off onto the boat—one would call it extremely safe. Who knew that later, on the boat, she could still flee at night? So when you take a concubine away from home, you should not only look into the girl’s family; you should also look into where the matchmaker lives, and have the innkeeper join in checking the facts, and only then will there be no loss. But in the main it is still safer to take a local girl.

stories.title_en: Boatmen Kill a Merchant Whose Copper Looked Like Treasure

paragraphs.zh: 罗四维，南京凤阳府临淮县人。同仆程三郎，带银一百餘两往松江买梭布，往福建建宁府卖，复往崇安买笋。其年笋少价贵，即将银在此处买走乌铜物，并三夹杯盘诸项铜器，用竹箱盛贮，并行李装作三担。崇安发夫，直到水口陈四店写船。陡遇表亲林子达，亦在此店中。达问：“买甚货物？”维曰：“只买些铜器去，更带杯盘等，欲留家用。”达同牙人陈四，代讨一箭船。舵公赖富二、水手李彩、翁暨得搬其行李上船，甚重，舵公疑是金银，乃起不良心，一上船后，再不搭人。维曰：“我要速去，何如不搭人？”舵公曰：“今将晚矣。明日随搭数人，便开船。”维叫三郎买些酒菜，今晚饮用。舵工与水手三人商议：“今晚错过机会，明日不好动手。”维与仆饮醉熟睡。半夜后，舵公将船移于闲处，三人将他主仆以刀砍死，丢尸于江。打开打看，乃是铜物，止现银壹十五两。富二曰：“我说都是银子，三人一场富贵。原来是这东西！”彩曰：“有这等好货物，也多值银。”富二曰：“发在何处去卖？”彩曰：“何愁无卖处？可安船在一处，沿途发卖，岂无人买？”
paragraphs.en: Luo Siwei was a man of Linhuai County in Fengyang Prefecture, under Nanjing. With his servant Cheng Sanlang he took a little more than a hundred taels, went to Songjiang to buy cotton cloth, sold it in Jianning Prefecture in Fujian, then went on to Chong’an to buy bamboo shoots. That year shoots were scarce and dear, so he used the silver there to buy blackened copperware, and also laminated cups and plates and other copper pieces. He packed them in bamboo chests, and with the luggage made three loads. From Chong’an he sent porters all the way to Chen Si’s shop at Shuikou to book a boat. There he suddenly met a cousin, Lin Zida, also in this shop. Zida asked: “What goods did you buy?” Siwei said: “Only some copperware to take, and also cups and plates I want to keep for the house.” Zida and the broker Chen Si hired an arrow-boat for him. The helmsman Lai Fuer and the sailors Li Cai and Weng Jide moved his luggage on board; it was very heavy. The helmsman suspected it was gold and silver, and a bad thought rose in him. Once they were on board he would take no more passengers. Siwei said: “I want to leave quickly—why take no one else?” The helmsman said: “It is almost evening now. Tomorrow we will take a few more and then cast off.” Siwei told Sanlang to buy some wine and food for tonight. The helmsman and the two sailors talked it over: “If we miss the chance tonight, tomorrow we cannot act.” Siwei and his servant drank themselves drunk and slept soundly. After midnight the helmsman moved the boat to a quiet spot; the three men cut master and servant to death with knives and threw the bodies in the river. They broke open the loads and looked: it was copperware, and only fifteen taels of ready silver. Fuer said: “I said it was all silver—a fortune for the three of us. And it turns out to be this stuff!” Cai said: “Goods this fine are still worth a good deal of silver.” Fuer said: “Where can we send them to sell?” Cai said: “Why worry about a place to sell? Moor the boat somewhere and sell along the way—will no one buy?”

paragraphs.zh: 林子达与四维分袂之后，已三个月矣，始到家中往拜四维。维父曰：“小儿出门，尚未归。”达曰：“差矣！”三月前，我在江西水口，同他在牙人陈四店相会。我与牙人同他去讨船，说他在福建买铜货，以竹箱装作三担，竟归来本处发脱。莫非舵公行歹意乎？”言未毕，父母妻子举家大哭。达曰：“且勿哭，倘在途中发卖也未可知。或舵公行歹意，必以铜物卖各处。试往各店踪迹铜物，问其来历，便见明白。纵铜物无踪，再到水口牙人陈四家，寻舵公问之，必得下落。”维父然之，叫次子罗逵随达去访。
paragraphs.en: It was already three months after Lin Zida had parted from Siwei when Zida reached home and went to call on Siwei. Siwei’s father said: “My son went out and has not yet come back.” Zida said: “That is wrong! Three months ago I met him at broker Chen Si’s shop at Shuikou in Jiangxi. I went with the broker to hire a boat for him. He said he had bought copper goods in Fujian, packed in bamboo chests as three loads, and was coming straight home to this place to sell them. Can it be the helmsman meant harm?” Before he had finished, father, mother, wife, and the whole house burst into tears. Zida said: “Do not cry yet. He may still be selling along the way, for all we know. Or if the helmsman meant harm, he would have to sell the copper in various places. Try tracing the copper in the shops, ask where it came from, and the matter will be clear. Even if the copper leaves no trace, go on to broker Chen Si’s at Shuikou, find the helmsman and question him, and you will surely get the bottom of it.” Siwei’s father agreed, and told his second son Luo Kui to go with Zida to inquire.

paragraphs.zh: 访至芜湖县，铺中见其铜物，即问：“此铜物是公自买的，抑或他客贩来发行的？”铺主曰：“三月前，有三个客人来卖者。”达曰：“何处人？”曰：“江西人。”达惊惶曰：“差矣，失手是实。”即同逵径至水口，问陈四曰：“前装表亲货物的舵公，是何处人？”陈四曰：“沿山县人。”达道其故，即同陈四到沿山捕捉。
paragraphs.en: They inquired as far as Wuhu County. In a shop they saw the copperware, and asked: “Did you buy this copper yourself, or did some other merchant bring it to sell?” The shopkeeper said: “Three months ago three guests came and sold it.” Zida said: “Men of what place?” He said: “Jiangxi men.” Zida was alarmed: “This is wrong—we have truly lost him.” He went with Kui straight to Shuikou and asked Chen Si: “The helmsman who loaded my cousin’s goods—what place was he from?” Chen Si said: “A man of Yanshan County.” Zida told him why, and went with Chen Si to Yanshan to seize them.

paragraphs.zh: 斯时，李彩、翁暨得卖得铜器，银入手，各在妓家去嫖。林、陈窥见彩，即躲之。林子达曰：“他在院中取乐，必不便动。我与你往县去告，差捕兵缉拿，恕不漏网。”二人入县告准，陈爷差捕兵六名，同林、陈往院中去捕缉。彩与得二人正与妓笑饮，陈四指与捕兵，俱擒锁之。再到赖富家来，富方出门他适，遇见亦被捉获。三人同拿到官，陈爷审问，将三人夹敲，受苦不过，只得招认。彩曰：“彼时搬箱上船，其重非常。疑是金银，三人方起意谋之，将尸丢落于江。开其箱看，尽是铜物，只得现银一拾五两，悔之无及。铜物沿途卖讫，银已分散。今其事败，是我等自作自受，甘认死罪。”陈爷将三人各打五十板，即拟典刑，赃追与罗逵、林子达领归。二人叩首而去。
paragraphs.en: At that time Li Cai and Weng Jide had sold the copperware, had the silver in hand, and had each gone to a brothel to wench. Lin and Chen caught sight of Cai and hid. Lin Zida said: “He is taking his pleasure in the house; he will not be in a hurry to move. You and I will go to the county to file a charge, and have constables sent to seize them, so they cannot slip the net.” The two went into the county; the charge was accepted. His Honor Chen sent six constables, who went with Lin and Chen to the brothel to arrest them. Cai and Jide were just laughing and drinking with the prostitutes; Chen Si pointed them out to the constables, and both were seized and locked. They then went to Lai Fu’s house; Fu was just going out elsewhere, met them, and was also caught. The three were taken together before the official. His Honor Chen examined them, put them in the ankle-press and beat them; they could not bear the pain and had to confess. Cai said: “At the time we moved the chests on board they were extraordinarily heavy. We thought it was gold and silver, so the three of us formed the intent to kill them, and threw the bodies in the river. We opened the chests and looked: all copperware, only fifteen taels of ready silver. Regret came too late. The copper was sold along the way; the silver has already been split. Now the affair is out; we brought it on ourselves, and willingly admit a capital crime.” His Honor Chen had each of the three given fifty strokes, then sentenced them to death; the stolen goods were recovered and given to Luo Kui and Lin Zida to take home. The two kowtowed and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：溪河本险危之地，舵公多蠢暴之徒。若带实银在身，须深藏严防。或带铜器铅锡等物，镇重类银，须明与说之，开与见之，以免其垂涎，方保安全。不然，逐金丸以弹雀，指薏苡为明珠，其不来奸人之睥睨者几希。若维仇之能报，犹幸子达之得其根脚也。使非因写船者以穷其舵公，何以歼罪人而殄厥慝乎？然诛逆何如保躬？死偿何如生还？故出行而带重物者，宜借鉴于斯而慎之密之，其永无失矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Streams and rivers are dangerous places by nature, and helmsmen are often coarse, violent men. If you carry ready silver on you, you must hide it deep and watch it strictly. If you carry copper, lead, tin, and the like—heavy things that resemble silver—you must tell them plainly, open the loads and show them, so they will not drool, and only then will you be safe. Otherwise it is like shooting sparrows with gold pellets, or pointing at coix seeds and calling them pearls: few will escape the greedy stares of villains. As for Siwei’s feud being avenged, it was still luck that Zida got the man’s origin. If they had not used the man who booked the boat to track down the helmsman, how could they have wiped out the guilty and cut off the evil? But punishing rebels is not as good as keeping your own person; death repaid is not as good as coming home alive. So those who travel and carry heavy goods should take a lesson from this, be careful and close, and they will never come to grief.

stories.title_en: Heavy Mirrors on Board Draw a Murder Plot

paragraphs.zh: 熊镐，章富人，乃世家子也。力足扼虎，兼习棍棒。尝月夜挟二婢往后园，遇一虎跳墙入，即退入家，各持钢叉、大杖出。虎对面扑来，镐以叉抵，顺放于地，急打一下。虎复再扑，镐又叉放之，再打一下，虎遂回身而去。镐从后赶打，虎为之倒。疾呼二婢曰：“速来助。”二婢各以大杖以鏖之，虎立死杖下。时称之曰“打虎镐四官”。
paragraphs.en: Xiong Hao of Zhangfu was a son of a hereditary official house. He was strong enough to hold a tiger, and had also practiced staff and club. Once on a moonlit night he took two maids to the back garden and met a tiger that had jumped over the wall. He went back into the house at once; each took a steel fork or a heavy staff and came out. The tiger sprang at them face to face; Hao blocked it with the fork, laid the fork down, and struck once. The tiger sprang again; Hao again used the fork and then struck once more; the tiger turned and left. Hao chased it from behind and beat it; the tiger fell. He quickly called the two maids: “Come help at once.” Each maid used a heavy staff and they laid on together; the tiger died under the staves. People at the time called him “Fourth Master Hao the Tiger-Beater.”

paragraphs.zh: 后思遍游各胜处，故脱兄云：“将出外买卖。”兄阻之曰：“汝刚而无谋，莫思赚钱，还恐生祸。”镐曰：“老仆满起有力多智，与我同去，何妨？”兄不能阻。镐带百餘金行，曰：“吾出外相机置货，虽不得利，岂折本乎？有谁人欺得我者！”及游浙粤，有货可买者，仆满起曰：“此价甚廉，买归必得利。”镐曰：“吾远到此，未遍览此中景致，若遂置货，安能轻身自由？”仆累禀几次，皆不见听，知其志在浪游，不思利也，后只任之，主饮亦饮，主行亦随。不半年，本去三分之二矣。起复曰：“不归将无盘缠。”镐曰：“本虽少，亦要置些货归，可当远回人事相送者。”又挨两月，到湖州，起又催归。镐曰：“买何物好？”起曰：“笔墨上好。”镐曰：“不在行不会拣择，恐受人亏。亦须更买甚物，与母嫂及我妻者？银本已折，省他辈多口。”起曰：“细缎、镜好。”镐曰：“细缎无多本，不是这般客。不如买十两笔墨，十两镜罢。”起曰：“亦好。”催趱买归，只两小箱。镐曰：“此货甚妙，又简便易带。”
paragraphs.en: Later he wanted to tour all the famous places, so he told his elder brother: “I am going out to trade.” His brother stopped him: “You are hard and have no cunning. Do not think of making money; I fear you will only make trouble.” Hao said: “The old servant Man Qi has strength and much wit; if he goes with me, what harm?” His brother could not stop him. Hao took a little more than a hundred taels and set out, saying: “I will go out and buy goods as the chance comes. Even if I make no profit, how should I lose the capital? Who can take advantage of me?” When they toured Zhejiang and Guangdong, and there were goods worth buying, the servant Man Qi said: “This price is very cheap; if we buy and take it home we will surely profit.” Hao said: “I have come a long way and have not yet seen all the sights here. If I buy goods at once, how can I travel light and free?” The servant reported it several times and was never heard; he knew his master’s mind was on idle touring, not on profit, and afterward only let him be: when the master drank, he drank; when the master went, he followed. In less than half a year two thirds of the capital was gone. Qi said again: “If we do not go home we will have no travel money.” Hao said: “Though the capital is small, we still must buy some goods to take back, to serve as gifts after a long journey.” They delayed another two months and reached Huzhou; Qi again urged him home. Hao said: “What should we buy?” Qi said: “Brushes and ink are best.” Hao said: “I am not in that trade and cannot choose; I fear I will be taken advantage of. We also need to buy something for Mother, my sister-in-law, and my wife. The capital is already lost; let us spare them extra talk.” Qi said: “Fine silks and mirrors would be good.” Hao said: “We have not much capital for silks; we are not that kind of merchant. Better buy ten taels of brushes and ink and ten taels of mirrors.” Qi said: “That will do too.” They hurried the purchase for the return; there were only two small chests. Hao said: “These goods are excellent, and also light and easy to carry.”

paragraphs.zh: 及到江边搭船，舵公见财主威仪，家人齐整，奈何行李只两小箱。及抬入船中，觉箱中镇重，想必尽是银也。故以言动问曰：“客官从何来，亦不多买些货物？”镐以本少，恐客商见轻，故谎言：“吾家兄敝任在湖广，吾从任中归，未买得甚货。”舵公曰：“原来是大舍。”又见家人伏侍恭敬，每呼主为相公，使用皆大手面，不与诸商一类，以此益信为真官舍，船中人皆敬让之。及到岸，诸商都搬起船。舵公独留熊大舍曰：“船中客官多，未能伸敬。念备一杯酒，敬请大舍。”即上岸，多买佳肴美酒，夜间劝饮，甚是殷勤，熊镐宽心放饮。舵公又苦劝家人酒。满起心知其非好意，初诈推不饮，后难禁其劝，亦饮数杯，推醉去睡。熊舍凭舵公劝饮，真醉不醒事。起俟其睡熟，即起对舵公曰：“吾非真醉。今将近家，心中忧闷，吃酒不下耳。此相公酒色之徒。大相公在任中，将几百两银打发他归。在路上嫖用都尽，只带得几把笔，几面镜归，与侄子辈作人事耳。明日大老爷归，必责我不能谏阻。世有此人，见酒如糖，又好夸口，怎么谏他？我试开两箱与你看，其中哪有厘银？”即取锁匙开两箱，惟笔与镜，并无银两。起取两面镜送舵公，曰：“一路来多蒙照顾，各送一镜与你用。”舵公曰：“主物不可擅送人。”起曰：“拿一半去，他也理不得，到家后那晓得数。”复锁住箱，与舵公去睡，起一夜提防。次日上岸，熊曰：“难得舵公如此好意，再偿他银一钱。”
paragraphs.en: When they hired a boat at the river, the helmsman saw a rich man’s bearing and servants in good order, yet the luggage was only two small chests. When they were lifted into the boat he felt how heavy the chests were, and thought they must be all silver. So he probed with words: “Where have you come from, sir? And you did not buy more goods?” Hao, because his capital was small, feared other merchants would look down on him, so he lied: “My elder brother holds a humble post in Huguang. I am returning from his post and did not buy much.” The helmsman said: “So you are a young gentleman.” He also saw the servants wait on him with respect, always calling their master “young sir,” and that he spent in a large style, not of a kind with ordinary merchants; for this he believed still more that he was truly a young gentleman of an official house, and everyone on the boat deferred to him. When they reached shore, the other merchants all moved off the boat. The helmsman alone kept Young Gentleman Xiong, saying: “There were many guests on the boat; I could not show respect. I have prepared a cup of wine; please let me invite you.” He went ashore, bought many fine dishes and good wine, pressed them to drink at night, most attentive; Xiong Hao drank with an easy heart. The helmsman also hard-pressed the servant to drink. Man Qi knew in his heart it was not kindly meant. At first he pretended to refuse; later he could not stop the urging, drank several cups, then pleaded drunkenness and went to sleep. Young Xiong let the helmsman press him, and was truly drunk and knew nothing. When Qi saw he was sound asleep, he got up and said to the helmsman: “I am not truly drunk. We are near home now; my heart is heavy, and I cannot get the wine down. This young master is a man of wine and women. The elder master, in his post, sent him home with several hundred taels. On the road he spent it all on whoring; he is only taking a few brushes and a few mirrors home as gifts for the nephews. Tomorrow the old master will come home and will surely blame me for not stopping him. There are men like this in the world: they see wine as sugar, and love to boast—how can I check him? Let me open the two chests and show you: is there a speck of silver in them?” He took the key and opened both chests: only brushes and mirrors, no silver at all. Qi took two mirrors and gave them to the helmsman, saying: “All along the way you have looked after us; I give each of you a mirror to use.” The helmsman said: “A master’s things must not be given away.” Qi said: “Take half; he will not be able to make it out, and once we are home he will not know the count.” He locked the chests again, went with the helmsman to sleep, and kept watch all night. The next day they went ashore. Hao said: “It is rare for a helmsman to be so kind; give him another qian of silver.”

paragraphs.zh: 及归家，起曰：“可数过镜，勿令有失。”镐检过曰：“更失两面。”起曰：“吾将这两面镜，换你我两颗头归。主人尚未知乎？”镐曰：“你何狂言？”起将船中劝饮事，一一叙之，曰：“彼非欲谋害，将别之人，何如此更费酒馔，若殷勤乎？”镐惊曰：“是也！非尔知事，险丧二命耳！”一家人闻之皆喜，赏满起。
paragraphs.en: When they reached home, Qi said: “Count the mirrors, so none are missing.” Hao checked and said: “Two more are gone.” Qi said: “I traded those two mirrors for your head and mine to come home. Does the master still not know?” Hao said: “Why this wild talk?” Qi told the affair of the drinking on the boat, item by item, and said: “If he did not mean to murder us, why would he spend extra on wine and food for other people, and be so attentive?” Hao was startled: “So it was! If you had not known how to act, we would nearly have lost two lives!” The whole household heard and was glad, and rewarded Man Qi.

paragraphs.zh: 按：镐本膏粱之子，以纵性为快，以夸口为高，哪知世路之险？若非满起心明，轻以二命付鱼腹耳。凡远行者，主若疏满，得一谨密家人，亦大有益。故旅以丧童仆为厉，以得童仆为吉。圣人系旅之义大矣哉。
paragraphs.en: Note: Hao was a son of rich food and fine clothes; he took following his nature as pleasure and boasting as high style, and did not know how dangerous the world’s roads are. If Man Qi had not had a clear mind, two lives would have been lightly given to the fishes’ bellies. Whenever you travel far, if the master is careless and slack, getting one close, careful servant is also a great benefit. So in the Travel hexagram, losing a servant is ominous, and gaining a servant is auspicious. How great is the Sage’s attached meaning for Travel!

stories.title_en: A Servant Puts the Bags on Another Boat by Mistake

paragraphs.zh: 陆梦麟，江西进贤人。往福建海澄县买胡椒十餘担，复往芜湖发卖。有一客伙，将硼砂一担对换，餘者以银伐之。次日，叫店家写舵公陈涯四船，直到建宁。诸货都搬入船，只一仆詹兴，挑实落行李一担，跟梦麟同行。途中陡遇一乡亲，动问家中事务，语喇喇不能休。乃命仆先担行李上船，再来此听使用。仆挑往别船去，收在船舱已讫，再来寻主，尚与乡亲谈叙未决。见仆来，即差之别干，始辞乡亲到船。查行李未见，即将家人打骂；又坐舵公偷去，状告本县胡爷，言舵公盗他卖胡椒银一百餘两，以店家祝念九作证。舵公诉：“船中有客商十数伙，哪见他仆挑行李上船？”胡爷拘来审问，同船众商都谈，未曾见挑甚行李。胡爷曰：“船不漏针。别货物都在，独行李有银便会失落？”将舵公敲夹，不认，曰：“是他仆詹兴见囊中有银，自盗去以陷我；或错担别船去，以致有失。小人虽夹死难招！”胡爷又审詹兴曰：“想是你错认别人船为己船，忙中有失，非你背主，好好招来免夹。”詹兴不认，乃夹敲一百。受苦不过，只得招认：“是主人路遇乡亲谈话，我自担上船去，藏入船舱讫，再回听主差唤。及到船，并未见行李。是我一时错认，以致有失。恐主人加罪于我，我故不敢承。望老爷救小人一命。”胡爷将詹兴责三十板，劝梦麟曰：“是你自错。凡出外为商，银物不可离身。当担行李时，须叫詹兴看守，待你到船，然后差别干；纵错上别船，亦不会失。今若此，是你命该失财，岂可以怨仆乎？”各发出免供。
paragraphs.en: Lu Menglin was a man of Jinxian in Jiangxi. He went to Haicheng County in Fujian, bought more than ten piculs of pepper, then went to Wuhu to sell it. A fellow merchant swapped a picul of borax; the rest was paid in silver. The next day he had the innkeeper book Helmsman Chen Yasi’s boat, going all the way to Jianning. All the goods were moved onto the boat; only one servant, Zhan Xing, carried a load of the real luggage and followed Menglin. On the way they suddenly met a fellow townsman; they asked about family affairs, and the talk rattled on and would not stop. So he ordered the servant to carry the luggage onto the boat first, then come back here and wait for orders. The servant carried it onto another boat, stowed it in the cabin, then came back to find his master, who was still talking with the townsman and had not finished. When he saw the servant come, he sent him on another errand, then took leave of the townsman and went to the boat. He checked and did not see the luggage, so he beat and cursed the servant; he also sat the theft on the helmsman, and filed a charge with His Honor Hu of the county, saying the helmsman had stolen more than a hundred taels of silver from the pepper sales, with innkeeper Zhu Nianjiu as witness. The helmsman stated: “There are a dozen-odd merchants on the boat; who saw his servant carry luggage on board?” His Honor Hu summoned them to hear the case; all the fellow merchants on the boat said they had not seen any luggage carried on. His Honor Hu said: “A boat does not leak a needle. The other goods are all here; only the luggage, which had silver, happens to be missing?” He put the helmsman in the press and beat him. The man would not confess, and said: “It was his servant Zhan Xing who saw there was silver in the bundle, stole it himself to trap me; or he carried it onto the wrong boat, and so it was lost. Even if you press this little man to death I will not confess!” His Honor Hu then examined Zhan Xing: “I think you mistook another man’s boat for your own, and in the hurry something was lost; it was not that you turned on your master. Confess properly and you will be spared the press.” Zhan Xing would not confess, so he was pressed and beaten a hundred blows. He could not bear the pain and had to confess: “My master met a fellow townsman on the road and was talking. I carried it onto a boat myself, hid it in the cabin, then went back to wait for my master’s orders. When we reached the boat, the luggage was not to be seen. I mistook it for a moment, and so it was lost. I feared my master would add to my punishment, so I dared not admit it. I beg Your Honor to spare this little man’s life.” His Honor Hu had Zhan Xing given thirty strokes, and advised Menglin: “This was your own mistake. Whenever you go out to trade, silver and goods must not leave your person. When the luggage was to be carried, you should have told Zhan Xing to watch it, and only sent him on other errands after you reached the boat; even if it went onto the wrong boat, it would not have been lost. Now that it has come to this, your fate was to lose the money—how can you resent the servant?” They were each sent out and spared further depositions.

paragraphs.zh: 按：货物上船，须不离人看守。要防舵公侵盗，又要得智仆为吉也。故雏仆之挑行节，银物所系，须跟在身边，托在实落，方无所失。若先令挑去，错寄别船，安能无失哉？然麟徒知叙旧之谈，致仆误丧其财而干讼者，何其愚也！诸商鉴此，可为后戒。
paragraphs.en: Note: When goods go onto a boat, you must not leave them unwatched. You have to guard against the helmsman stealing, and you also need a smart servant to be lucky. So when a greenhorn servant carries the travel bundle—the thing silver and goods hang on—he must follow at your side, and you must leave it only where it is secure, and then nothing will be lost. If you first tell him to carry it ahead, and it is wrongly left on another boat, how can there be no loss? Yet Menglin only knew how to talk over old times, and caused the servant to lose the money by mistake and drag them into a lawsuit—how foolish! Merchants should look at this and take it as a later warning.

stories.title_en: A Porter Dashes Off with Unloaded Cargo

paragraphs.zh: 建城溪边，凡客船到岸，众脚夫丛集，求雇担代挑入城。有老成客，必喝退众夫，待船货齐收上岸，都数纪定，然后分作几担，叫几名脚夫，自相识认，乃发入城，急令人跟行其后，方保无失。若雏家到，众脚夫不管物件检齐否，即为收拾上担，及急跟夫去，多致遗物在船中未尽收。
paragraphs.en: By the creek at Jianning city, whenever a guest boat reaches shore, porters swarm and beg to be hired to carry loads into the city. An experienced traveler will always shout the crowd of porters back, wait until the boat’s goods are all brought ashore and counted and recorded, then divide them into several loads, call several porters he can recognize, send them into the city, and at once have someone follow behind; only then is there no loss. If a greenhorn arrives, the porters, without waiting to see whether the things have been fully checked, pack them onto the poles at once; and if you hurry after the porters, you often leave things still on the boat not yet brought in.

paragraphs.zh: 有侯官县一田秀才，出外作馆。年冬归，得束金四十餘两，衣被物件亦十餘两，共作两大笼。经过建城，欲入拜乡亲，命一脚夫挑笼先行。田乃儒家，从后缓步随之。脚夫见其来迟，一步紧一步，趱入城门；人闹攘处，更是疾行，遂挑入曲巷逃走。田从后虽叫“止步”，哪能止得！入城曲巷多歧，何处可寻？次日，往府吕巡捕呈之。
paragraphs.en: There was a licentiate Tian of Houguan County who had gone out to teach. At year’s end he was going home; he had more than forty taels of teaching silver, and clothes and bedding worth another ten-odd taels, packed as two large baskets. Passing Jianning, he wanted to go in and call on a fellow townsman, and ordered a porter to carry the baskets ahead. Tian was a Confucian scholar, and followed slowly behind. The porter, seeing him come late, walked faster and faster, hurried in at the city gate; in the crowded press he went still quicker, then carried the load into a winding alley and fled. Though Tian called from behind, “Stop!” how could he stop him? Inside the city the winding alleys forked many ways—where could one search? The next day he presented the matter to Prefectural Constable Lü.

paragraphs.zh: 吕捕衙是精明官，以脚扶拐物，须用脚夫查之。即叫二差人来：“你认定这田相公，今午后穿白长衫在船中。行李到，必有脚夫挑走，你二人从后密跟，到他家拿来。”再对秀才曰：“你今再讨假行李一担，在十里外搭船来府，照前日到岸时，叫脚夫来挑。你穿白长衫去，此两差人易认。若已在旁，你故意缓行，任此脚夫挑去，必能拿得前脚夫来。”秀才未会其意。
paragraphs.en: Constable Lü was a sharp official. To catch a porter who had made off with goods, you must use porters to find him. He at once called two runners: “You mark this Licentiate Tian. This afternoon he will wear a white long gown on a boat. When luggage arrives, a porter will surely run off with it; you two follow secretly behind and seize him at his house.” He then said to the licentiate: “Today get a dummy load of luggage, board a boat ten li out, and come to the prefecture. When you reach shore as you did the other day, call a porter to carry it. Wear a white long gown so these two runners can know you. If they are already beside you, walk slowly on purpose and let this porter carry it off; they will surely catch the earlier porter.” The licentiate did not yet see his meaning.

paragraphs.zh: 即日下午，备行李从十里外搭船到，见此两美人在旁，各相认得，故叫脚夫挑行李，从后缓随。脚夫果然挑走。二公差迤跟到家拿住，曰：“吕爷叫你。”脚夫黄三不知来历，只得随往。吕爷曰：“你缘何挑走秀才行李？”黄三惊曰：“只暂寄我家，便欲送还。”官止喝：“打五板！”田秀才方到衙。吕爷叮咛黄三曰：“今日饶你罪。这田相公昨日被脚夫挑走一担笼，限你两日代根究来；若寻不出，定坐你赔。”黄三曰：“河下挑夫，两日换一班。昨日不是我辈。”吕爷曰：“你即根究昨日的。”
paragraphs.en: That same afternoon he prepared luggage, boarded a boat ten li out, and arrived. He saw the two runners beside him; each knew the other, so he called a porter to carry the luggage and followed slowly behind. The porter indeed ran off with it. The two runners followed at a distance to his house and seized him, saying: “His Honor Lü wants you.” The porter, Huang San, did not know why, and had to go along. His Honor Lü said: “Why did you run off with the licentiate’s luggage?” Huang San, startled, said: “I was only going to leave it at my house for a while, then send it back.” The official merely shouted, “Give him five strokes!” Licentiate Tian then reached the yamen. His Honor Lü instructed Huang San: “Today I spare you. Yesterday a porter ran off with one load of this Tian’s baskets. I give you two days to track him down; if you cannot find him, you will certainly be made to pay.” Huang San said: “The porters on the river change shifts every two days. Yesterday was not our shift.” His Honor Lü said: “Then you track down yesterday’s men.”

paragraphs.zh: 黄三密访两日，不能得。第三日，公差来拿。到半途，见一脚夫柳五，将银三钱换钱用，随即买鱼肉等归家。黄三再拿到衙，禀曰：“并访不得。只今遇柳五换钱，多买鱼肉，事有可疑。”捕衙立差四人，同田秀才、黄三直往柳五家搜。只一间小房，搜果见赃。拿到捕衙，柳五供曰：“银物现在。前五日未敢出门，今日止用银三钱换钱，买物作欢。拐盗是实。”捕衙发打二十板，曰：“你二脚夫拐资客货，各该拟徒。但黄三捕出柳五，以此赎罪，再打十板释放，以惩后日。姑念柳五穷汉，只拟不应罪，纳完发放。”再叫田秀才具领状来，尽将原物领去。不数日，拿得真赃正犯，非有治才，安能如此哉！
paragraphs.en: Huang San inquired in secret for two days and could not find him. On the third day runners came to seize him. Halfway, he saw a porter, Liu Wu, changing three qian of silver into cash, then at once buying fish, meat, and such to take home. Huang San had him seized as well and taken to the yamen, and reported: “I could find nothing. Only just now I met Liu Wu changing money and buying a good deal of fish and meat; the matter looks suspicious.” The constable at once sent four men, who went with Licentiate Tian and Huang San straight to Liu Wu’s house to search. There was only one small room; they searched and indeed found the loot. They took him to the constable’s yamen. Liu Wu stated: “The silver and goods are here. For the past five days I dared not go out. Today I only used three qian of silver to change money and buy things to make merry. The theft is real.” The constable ordered twenty strokes, and said: “You two porters made off with a traveler’s goods; each of you ought to be sentenced to penal servitude. But Huang San caught Liu Wu, so that redeems his crime; give him ten more strokes and release him, as a warning for later days. I will be lenient to Liu Wu as a poor fellow: sentence him only for doing what he ought not, and when the fine is paid let him go.” He then told Licentiate Tian to file a receipt, and all the original goods were given back to him. In a few days they had caught the true thief with the true loot. Without a talent for governing, how could it have been done like this?

paragraphs.zh: 按：脚夫挑走货物，处处有之，故出行最宜慎防。若吕捕衙之发奸得捕盗不遗余力者，全在以脚夫查脚夫一着。所谓“以蛮夷攻蛮夷”是也。又谚云“贼拿贼，针挑刺”，亦此意也。雇夫者可以为戒，捕盗者可以为法。
paragraphs.en: Note: Porters running off with goods happen everywhere, so when you travel you should most carefully guard against it. As for Constable Lü’s exposing the fraud and catching the thief with no effort spared, the whole thing lay in that one move of using a porter to find a porter. This is what is meant by “using barbarians to attack barbarians.” The proverb also says, “Set a thief to catch a thief; use a needle to pick out a splinter”—the same idea. Those who hire porters may take it as a warning; those who catch thieves may take it as a method.
